intent: understand closing line value as a process metric
title: Closing line value: how to calculate it and track it honestly
seoTitle: Closing Line Value: Formula, Examples and Tracking Sheet
description: Calculate closing line value with worked examples, distinguish price CLV from a no-vig closing benchmark, and copy a practical tracking sheet.
dek: Compare the price you took with the same market at close. Then check which CLV calculation you are using, because price improvement and a no-vig benchmark can tell different stories.
author: chris-habib

verdict: For the same selection, divide entry decimal odds by closing decimal odds and subtract one to get price-based CLV. Label the formula, keep a consistent closing reference and record missing closes. A better quoted price is not proof of profit.

faqs.question: How do you calculate closing line value?
faqs.answer: For the exact same selection and settlement rules, price-based CLV is entry decimal odds divided by closing decimal odds, minus one. Multiply by 100 for a percentage. State the formula and closing reference because other calculations also use the CLV label.

faqs.question: Does positive CLV guarantee profit?
faqs.answer: No. A better quoted price can still be worse than a no-vig closing benchmark, and the closing benchmark itself can be wrong. A selection with positive CLV can lose.

faqs.question: Can I compare CLV when a prop line changes?
faqs.answer: Not with a simple price-only ratio across different thresholds. Record both lines and prices. Find a closing price at the original threshold or mark the comparison unavailable.
